title: Drugs for Allergic Reactions
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Allergic Reactions and Pharmacology
headings.content: Allergic reactions represent an immune system overreaction to typically harmless environmental substances known as allergens. When a sensitized individual encounters an allergen, IgE antibodies trigger mast cells and basophils to release inflammatory mediators like histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes. This rapid degranulation causes classic allergic symptoms ranging from mild rhinitis and urticaria to life-threatening systemic anaphylaxis characterized by bronchospasm and severe hypotension. Pharmacology in allergy management focuses on interrupting this inflammatory cascade at various points. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these mechanisms is vital for anticipating pharmacotherapeutic interventions in both emergency and routine outpatient settings. Drugs utilized in allergy treatment include antihistamines, corticosteroids, sympathomimetics, mast cell stabilizers, and leukotriene receptor antagonists. Each class targets specific pathways of the immune response to alleviate symptoms, prevent tissue damage, and restore physiological stability. Recognizing the pharmacological classification and primary action of these medications ensures safe medication administration and effective patient monitoring across diverse healthcare environments.

headings.title: Antihistamines: Classification and Mechanism of Action
headings.content: Antihistamines are foundational drugs in the management of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and mild allergic manifestations. They work primarily by competitively blocking histamine at H1-receptor sites, thereby preventing histamine from binding and exerting its vasodilatory, bronchoconstrictive, and pruritic effects. Antihistamines are broadly classified into first-generation and second-generation agents. First-generation antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine and chlorpheniramine, readily cross the blood-brain barrier. This central nervous system penetration accounts for their prominent side effect profile, which includes significant sedation, drowsiness, and anticholinergic effects like dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention. Consequently, they require caution in elderly populations and individuals operating machinery. In contrast, second-generation antihistamines, such as cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine, are peripherally selective. They do not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, making them non-sedating or minimally sedating while still providing potent peripheral H1 blockade. Nursing students must understand these distinctions to educate patients accurately regarding dosing schedules, potential side effects, and activities to avoid while taking these medications.

headings.title: Corticosteroids in Allergy Management
headings.content: Corticosteroids are potent anti-inflammatory agents utilized extensively in moderate to severe allergic reactions, asthma exacerbations, and chronic allergic conditions. They exert their therapeutic effects by binding to intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, which subsequently downregulates the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and inhibits the synthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes. By suppressing both the early and late phases of the allergic response, corticosteroids effectively reduce tissue edema, leukocyte infiltration, and mucosal inflammation. Depending on the clinical presentation, they can be administered via various routes, including topical creams for contact dermatitis, intranasal sprays for allergic rhinitis, oral tablets for moderate allergic flare-ups, and intravenous or intramuscular injections for acute severe reactions. While highly effective, systemic corticosteroid therapy carries significant potential for adverse effects when used long-term, including adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, weight gain, osteoporosis, and increased susceptibility to infections. Nurses must monitor patients for these complications, encourage appropriate tapering schedules to prevent acute adrenal insufficiency, and educate patients on proper administration techniques, such as rinsing the mouth after using inhaled corticosteroids to prevent oral candidiasis.

headings.title: Epinephrine and Emergency Treatment of Anaphylaxis
headings.content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid airway compromise, hypotension, and circulatory collapse. Epinephrine is the absolute first-line drug of choice for anaphylaxis and must be administered immediately upon recognition of symptoms. As a potent non-selective alpha and beta adrenergic agonist, epinephrine rapidly reverses life-threatening signs: alpha-1 receptor stimulation causes intense vasoconstriction, which increases blood pressure and reduces upper airway mucosal edema; beta-1 receptor stimulation increases heart rate and myocardial contractility; and beta-2 receptor stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscles to relieve bronchospasm and wheezing. The standard route for emergency administration is intramuscular (IM) injection into the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh, which provides faster and more reliable absorption than subcutaneous delivery. Nurses must be proficient in calculating doses, utilizing auto-injectors like the EpiPen, and monitoring vital signs continuously. Because a biphasic reaction can occur hours after the initial event, patients must be observed in a clinical setting for an appropriate duration following epinephrine administration and stabilization.

headings.title: Mast Cell Stabilizers and Leukotriene Modulators
headings.content: Mast cell stabilizers and leukotriene modulators represent essential classes of prophylactic medications used in the long-term management of chronic allergic conditions, particularly asthma and allergic rhinitis. Mast cell stabilizers, such as cromolyn sodium, work by inhibiting the degranulation of sensitized mast cells, thereby preventing the release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other inflammatory mediators when an allergen is encountered. They are primarily used for prophylaxis and must be taken regularly before exposure to triggers, as they possess no direct bronchodilatory or acute rescue properties. Leukotriene modulators, such as montelukast, either inhibit the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme or selectively block leukotriene receptors. Leukotrienes are potent inflammatory chemicals released from mast cells and eosinophils that induce sustained bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and airway edema. By blocking their action, montelukast reduces airway inflammation and improves lung function in chronic asthma and allergic rhinitis. Nursing students must recognize that these medications are not intended for acute rescue situations like an asthma attack or anaphylaxis, and patient adherence to daily preventive dosing is critical for therapeutic success.

headings.title: Nursing Assessments and Administration Considerations
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessments and meticulous administration considerations are paramount when managing patients receiving anti-allergic pharmacotherapy. Prior to administering any allergy medication, nurses must conduct a thorough allergy history, review current medications to screen for potential drug-drug interactions, and obtain baseline vital signs and respiratory assessments, including lung sounds and oxygen saturation. For patients receiving intravenous or parenteral agents, monitoring for hypersensitivity infusion reactions is essential. When administering emergency drugs like epinephrine, nurses must verify the correct dosage, concentration, and route, ensuring rapid access to resuscitation equipment. In outpatient and hospital settings alike, nurses play a vital role in evaluating treatment efficacy, watching for adverse drug reactions such as excessive sedation from first-generation antihistamines or paradoxical bronchospasm, and documenting patient responses accurately. Furthermore, nurses must collaborate with multidisciplinary healthcare teams to adjust dosages based on renal or hepatic function, particularly in vulnerable populations such as pediatric and geriatric patients across Nigerian clinical settings.

headings.title: Patient Education and Prevention of Allergic Triggers
headings.content: Patient education and the prevention of allergic triggers form the cornerstone of long-term allergy management and reduction of recurrent healthcare admissions. Nurses are pivotal educators, empowering patients and their families to identify and eliminate exposure to common environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold, pet dander, and specific foods or insect stings. Education must cover proper environmental control measures, such as using air conditioning, washing bedding in hot water, and avoiding outdoor activities during high pollen counts. For patients with severe systemic allergies, comprehensive education must include instruction on how to recognize early prodromal symptoms of anaphylaxis, how to properly store and utilize epinephrine auto-injectors, and the absolute necessity of carrying the device at all times. Patients should also be advised to wear medical alert identification jewelry and to seek immediate emergency medical care following the use of an epinephrine auto-injector, keeping in mind the risk of biphasic reactions. Through clear, culturally sensitive communication, nurses ensure that patients understand their medication regimens, recognize warning signs, and maintain active control over their health.
